title: Resources
text: A curated set of resources for the built environment, urban economics, and teaching. I add to these lists as I find more. Most of the data sources are free, and many can be downloaded at the census-tract or metro level.

title: Resources
text:
Regenerative development & sustainability



A collection of resources about the environment, with a particular focus on the built environment, for students and researchers interested in regenerative solutions to city building, transportation, and other built-environment problems.

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change The IPCC’s assessment reports on the science of climate change. A Green New Deal (2008) New Economics Foundation’s original Green New Deal report (archived). Regenesis Group Pioneers of regenerative development and design practice. International Living Future Institute Home of the Living Building Challenge. U.S. Green Building Council The LEED rating system and green-building education. Capital Institute Regenerative economics and the principles of a regenerative economy. Doughnut Economics Action Lab Tools for cities applying Kate Raworth’s doughnut framework. CityCraft Foundation Regenerative city-building in West Denver and beyond. Sun Valley EcoDistrict Master plan for a 100-acre Denver neighborhood guided by the EcoDistricts Protocol (Shears Adkins Rockmore). Sun Valley Redevelopment (DHA) Denver Housing Authority’s replacement of 333 public housing units with 940 new mixed-income homes and an 11-acre riverfront park.

ESG & sustainable investment

GRESB The ESG benchmark for real estate and infrastructure portfolios. CRREM Carbon Risk Real Estate Monitor: decarbonization pathways and stranding-risk tools for buildings. Principles for Responsible Investment The UN-supported investor network for integrating ESG into investment decisions. ISSB (IFRS Sustainability Standards) Global baseline standards for sustainability and climate-related financial disclosure. Global Reporting Initiative Widely used standards for corporate sustainability reporting.

Circular economy & embodied carbon

Ellen MacArthur Foundation Circular-economy principles, case studies, and design for cities. Circularity Gap Report Circle Economy’s annual measure of how circular the global economy is. Building Transparency (EC3) Free calculator for the embodied carbon of construction materials. Architecture 2030 Targets and tools for cutting operational and embodied carbon in the built environment.

Resiliency frameworks

Resilient Cities Network The successor network to the Rockefeller Foundation’s 100 Resilient Cities. UN SDGs — 2019 U.S. Cities Report How the 100 largest U.S. metros perform on the Sustainable Development Goals. Colorado Resiliency Office State resources for community resilience planning.

title: Resources
text:
Data sources

Real estate, housing & the economy

FRED Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis — thousands of economic series, including rates, home prices, and metro data. data.census.gov American Community Survey and decennial census tables down to the block group. HUD User datasets Fair Market Rents, income limits, CHAS affordability data, and LIHTC properties. FHFA House Price Index Repeat-sales home price indexes for the nation, states, metros, counties, and ZIP codes. Zillow Research data Home value (ZHVI) and rent (ZORI) indexes, inventory, and sales data. Census building permits Monthly and annual new residential construction permits by metro and place. Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment, wages, CPI, and construction-cost data. World Development Indicators The World Bank’s cross-country data on economies, urbanization, and the environment. BEA regional data GDP and personal income by state, county, and metro area. NCREIF The NCREIF Property Index and other institutional real estate performance benchmarks. Nareit data & research REIT index returns, market capitalization, and sector data. NLIHC — Out of Reach The housing wage needed to afford a modest rental in every state, metro, and county. Eviction Lab Eviction filing data and tracking for U.S. cities and states (Princeton).



Spatial, urban & transportation

IPUMS Harmonized census and survey microdata (USA, CPS, international). NHGIS Historical census tables and GIS boundary files from 1790 to the present. Census TIGER/Line Shapefiles for tracts, block groups, roads, and places. LEHD / LODES Where people live and work: block-level origin–destination employment data. EPA Smart Location Database Density, land-use diversity, street design, and transit access for every block group. National Zoning Atlas Standardized, mappable zoning codes across U.S. jurisdictions. Urban Institute Data Catalog Datasets from Urban’s housing, finance, and neighborhood research.



Climate, energy & environment

NOAA NCEI Historical climate and weather data, including temperature and precipitation records. Climate Mapping for Resilience & Adaptation County-level projections of heat, drought, flooding, and wildfire. ENERGY STAR benchmarking Portfolio Manager, the standard tool for measuring building energy and water use. USGBC project directory Searchable directory of LEED-certified projects and their scorecards.



Denver & Colorado

Denver Open Data Catalog City and County of Denver datasets: parcels, zoning, permits, and more. Colorado Information Marketplace The State of Colorado’s open data portal. DRCOG Regional Data Catalog Denver Regional Council of Governments data on land use, transportation, and growth. State Demography Office Colorado population estimates and forecasts by county and municipality.

title: Resources
text:
Discussion-based teaching



I use discussion in my topics class, Triple Bottom Line and the Built Environment, to encourage students to engage deeply with material on social justice and environmental sustainability — including by facilitating their own class discussions. As Brookfield and Preskill describe it, the purposes of discussion are fourfold: (1) to help participants reach a more critically informed understanding of the topic, (2) to enhance their self-awareness and capacity for self-critique, (3) to foster an appreciation for the diversity of opinion that emerges when viewpoints are exchanged openly and honestly, and (4) to act as a catalyst for taking informed action in the world.

Stephen Brookfield’s website Works, resources, and tools for facilitating discussion and adult learning, including the Critical Incident Questionnaire. DU Office of Teaching and Learning Resources for teaching and for using technology to support learning. The Discussion Book: 50 Great Ways to Get People Talking A one-page summary of the book’s 50 methods (Columbia CTL).


Brookfield, S. D., & Preskill, S. (2005). Discussion as a Way of Teaching: Tools and Techniques for Democratic Classrooms. John Wiley & Sons.

More teaching resources I recommend

Liberating Structures Simple facilitation methods that get every voice in the room into the conversation. Project Zero Thinking Routines Harvard’s short, repeatable routines that make student thinking visible. CORE Econ Free, modern economics textbooks built around real-world problems and data. Gapminder Interactive data tools and lesson materials for teaching with global data. Starting Point: Teaching Economics SERC’s collection of active-learning techniques and examples for economics. Eberly Center (Carnegie Mellon) Evidence-based teaching principles and strategies for course design.

title: Andrew G. Mueller
text:
About
I am an Associate Professor in the Franklin L. Burns School of Real Estate and Construction Management, part of the Daniels College of Business at the University of Denver. My research uses the tools of applied microeconomics to real estate finance, sustainability, and urban economics — including real estate market cycles and investment, sustainable and regenerative development in the built environment, and the economics of housing affordability.
I hold a Ph.D. in Economics from Colorado State University and an M.S. in Real Estate and Construction Management from the University of Denver, and I bring two decades of industry experience in real estate research, development, and investment to my academic work.
I am also a regenerative practitioner: I bring regenerative development principles to community-engaged projects in the Denver region, from the DU Grand Challenges sustainability cohort to the Community Integrated Research Center. You can read more about that work on the Engagement page.

title: Teaching
text: I teach real estate and built-environment courses at the University of Denver, with an emphasis on social justice and environmental sustainability in the built environment. My classes lean on discussion-based learning to help students engage deeply with the material, and I use classroom technology to give students the chance to share their work with the world.

text:
Student projects



In Triple Bottom Line and the Built Environment, students build public websites around their work:


Graduate · REAL 4000
Students choose a critical issue related to the built environment, outline the primary challenges, discuss how the issue affects the City of Denver, and propose a plan of action for Denver to address it.


Undergraduate · REAL 1700
Students identify a parcel of land in the Denver metro region and propose a redevelopment — a regenerative feasibility study covering stakeholder engagement, a theoretical LEED rating, and the financing of green enhancements.

title: Research
text:
My research applies the tools of applied microeconomics to questions in real estate finance, sustainability, and urban economics. A recurring theme is how the built environment can move toward regenerative development — projects and policies that restore environmental and social systems rather than merely reducing harm. Related strands of my work examine real estate market cycles and investment strategy, the economics of housing affordability, environmental and social (ESG) performance in real estate, and the links between zoning, urban form, and travel behavior.
For published, peer-reviewed work, see Publications. Current working papers are listed below; drafts are available on request.

title: Research
text:
Working papers





ESG Machine learning

Assessing the Consistency of REIT ESG Scores Relative to ESG Reports
With B. Williams and A. Holder.

Uses textual analysis and machine learning to evaluate how consistently the ESG scores assigned to real estate investment trusts (REITs) reflect the content of the firms’ own ESG reports.









Regenerative development

Towards Regenerative Development: Adopting Principles and Measuring Outcomes in Real Estate Projects

Develops a framework for applying regenerative development principles in real estate, and proposes ways to measure the environmental and social outcomes of projects that adopt them.









Housing Affordability

Nowhere to Sleep at the Bottom: The Plight of Housing Affordability for the Lowest Earners in the U.S.
With T. J. PlaHovinsak and L. Terschan.

Examines housing affordability for the lowest-income households in the United States and the structural gaps that leave the bottom of the market underserved.









Capital markets International

Global Capital Flows to Real Estate
With S. Laposa and G. R. Mueller.

Investigates the macroeconomic and cross-border determinants of capital flows into real estate, drawing on lessons from the foreign direct investment literature.

title: Engagement
text: As a regenerative practitioner, I work to apply regenerative development principles — restoring environmental and social systems rather than simply reducing harm — through community-engaged scholarship in and around Denver. Below are several initiatives I have helped lead.

title: Engagement
section: Environmental Sustainability in an Urban Context
text:
Environmental Sustainability in an Urban Context
I co-led the Environmental Sustainability in an Urban Context cohort of the DU Grand Challenges (2018–2021). Each Grand Challenges cohort spends its first year in a collective-impact process to determine the group’s goals; the Sustainability Cohort set an overarching objective to deepen the DU community’s involvement with community partners, organized around four pilot projects.

title: Engagement
text:
Community Integrated Research Center (CIRC)
The Community Integrated Research Center (CIRC) was created as part of the CityCraft initiative to bring scholars from across Colorado’s Front Range together to help the City and County of Denver redevelop West Denver in a regenerative way. The group includes members of the CityCraft team along with CU Denver’s Urban Planning Department, DU’s Real Estate and Construction Management Department, Colorado State University’s Institute for the Built Environment, and Regis University’s Business School.
